extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, parties, and hearing examiners participating in Montana administrative agency contested cases
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, sample forms, and procedural standards for litigating contested cases before Montana agencies (petitions, motions, pre-hearing practice, evidence, notices, subpoenas, protective orders, exceptions, judicial review, and declaratory rulings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to counsel in agency proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to counsel is recognized in agency proceedings; the right "should be uniformly recognized for all state agencies." The last qualification inserted states that the provision "shall not be construed" to require the agency to furnish counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize parties' right to be represented; note legislative history showing uniform recognition. The statute's qualification makes clear agencies are not required to provide counsel free of charge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted non-attorney representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies may permit representation by non-attorneys (e.g., Rule 46-2.2-P240 of Dept. of Social and Rehabilitation Services permits, under certain circumstances, a medical provider to represent a recipient; the Public Service Commission permits Class B Interstate Commerce Commission practitioners who are not attorneys to represent others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check agency-specific rules to determine who may represent parties; examples show differing agency practices and the need to consult cross-references and precedent (citing County of Blaine v. Moore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of pleadings standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Except where a statute expressly provides to the contrary, service in all agency proceedings subject to this part and in proceedings for judicial review shall be as prescribed for civil actions in the district courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, Rule 5 M.R.C.P. (service of subsequent pleadings; certificate of mailing) is generally used for administrative pleadings once a matter becomes contested. Rule 4 (summons) is not often appropriate for administrative contested cases but is used for petitions for judicial review after final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings construed to do substantial justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative pleadings shall be construed to do substantial justice and technical standards of pleading are relatively unimportant to administrative procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use common-sense solutions to pleading problems; avoid over-emphasis on technical pleading form — substantive justice is prioritized (citing Western Bank of Billings v. State Banking Board).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and effect of the part; nonpreemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in this part shall be considered to limit or repeal requirements imposed by statute or otherwise recognized law. No subsequent legislation shall be considered to supersede or modify any provision of this part, whether by implication or otherwise, except to the extent that such legislation shall do so expressly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the part as preserving existing statutory requirements; do not assume later statutes modify these provisions unless they expressly say so. Repeal clause: repeal inconsistent parts of law to extent of conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for establishing public convenience and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether approval of a transfer of an all-beverage license will serve the public convenience and necessity, the department may consider such factors as: (a) the number of all-beverage licenses presently serving the area in relation to the population of the area, as this ratio compares to such ratios in comparable communities; (b) adequacy of existing services in the neighborhood or portion of the quota area into which transfer is proposed; (c) socio-economic trends in the area; (d) any special services (such as meeting facilities or restaurant service) proposed to be offered in conjunction with beverage sales, which special services would satisfy unmet demands in the quota area; and (e) safe and adequate parking and traffic access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support applications with affidavits or pre-filed written testimony addressing these specific factors; agencies may adopt rules reflecting these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and form of a petition to amend a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to amend a rule should identify the petitioner, state the interest represented, set out the proposed amendment text, and assert the authority and reasons for the change (e.g., that the amendment will aid efficient administration and focus hearings on relevant issues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include petitioner name/address, constituency being represented, statutory authority for rulemaking, proposed rule language (with changes marked), and an explanation of why the amendment is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit evidence for public convenience and necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits supporting public convenience and necessity should state the affiant's residence and length of residency, employment and qualifications, familiarity with the locale, and specific reasons why the proposed facility would serve public convenience and necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete factual statements (residence, employment, personal observations) and explain how the proposed establishment meets local needs; affidavit form shows numbered narrative factual paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and pleading for intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition to intervene should set out grounds for intervention, describing how the intervenor's welfare or interests would be adversely affected by the applicant's proposal (e.g., that the proposed relocation would not be justified and would harm neighborhood welfare).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State specific facts and legal grounds supporting intervention; file timely and include representative's signature and address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing conference objectives and subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-hearing conference is called to consider simplification of issues by consent of the parties, hearing preliminary motions, and formulating a schedule. Parties should be prepared to identify and consider matters including: (a) facts which parties may agree are true and require no proof; (b) issues of fact and law; (c) amendments to the application; (d) exhibits which may be introduced; (e) witnesses which may be called; (f) pre-hearing motions; and (g) pre-hearing discovery desired, if any.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conference to stipulate exhibits to be admitted without proof and to set procedural deadlines; be ready to discuss streamlining and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing order contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-hearing order should list witnesses each party will call, joint exhibits stipulated by the parties, exhibits each party will offer, deadlines for discovery requests, and the date/time/location the hearing will commence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare witness lists and exhibit lists in advance; include specific discovery cut-off dates and location details; use the order to fix the hearing logistics and limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and contents of subpoenas (deposition and appearance)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subpoena should direct the person to appear for deposition or hearing at a specified time/place and, where appropriate, command production of specified documents (e.g., financial records); failure to appear may result in court enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note agencies may have different subpoena forms and separate forms for subpoena duces tecum; include certificate of service and copy to all parties of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and scope for protective orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A protective order may be entered to protect a party from annoyance, embarrassment, or to prevent conflict between privacy and public disclosure (Rule 26(C), M.R.C.P.). The moving party may request that certain records not be inquired into or that discovery be limited to a neutral expert who will answer only questions relevant to specified issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protective orders can limit access (e.g., financial records), require selection of a neutral accountant at party expense, and restrict questioning to relevant matters; provide proposed protective order language specifying the limitations and procedure for neutral examiner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion to take official notice
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may move the department to take official notice of specific facts (e.g., number and type of licenses issued, applicable department rules) by stating facts to be noticed and the basis for noticing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft the motion listing each fact proposed to be noticed with supporting citations or explanations; include certificate of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to contest a fact proposed to be officially noticed
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may move to contest a fact proposed to be officially noticed, alleging specific grounds why the noticed fact is incorrect or disputable (e.g., asserting that some licenses do not meet the definition relied upon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State precise factual or definitional objections, cite authority (e.g., industry definitions), and request opportunity to present contrary evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing exceptions to proposed decision
rubrics_metrics.description: An aggrieved party may file exceptions to a hearing examiner's proposed decision, pointing out omissions (e.g., absence of required findings such as anticipated profit margin) or findings unsupported by the weight of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify each exception with citation to transcript or record pages where contradictions or omissions appear; request corrective relief or further findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit for disqualification (personal bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit for disqualification should be timely filed under the statutory provision (82-4211, R.C.M. 1947) and state specific grounds of personal bias or relationship (e.g., familial ties to a party and prior testimony) which demonstrate inability to have a fair and impartial hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include oath, detailed factual allegations supporting bias, a request for disqualification, and a request that any refusal to disqualify be made part of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and content for petition for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for judicial review should identify the petitioner as aggrieved, name the agency and respondents, state the final decision and date, and allege grounds for relief such as that the decision is clearly erroneous in view of the reliable, probative, and substantial evidence on the whole record; that the decision omits essential findings requested by a party; or that the decision is arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pray for relief such as reversal of the agency order and any other proper relief. Note: economic losses of a competitor are probably not grounds to decline issuance of a liquor license (practical caveat).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of proposed suspension (required contents and respondent rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of proposed suspension must state the hearing date/time/location, statutory and rule authority for the suspension, the alleged violation(s) (with specifics where possible), and inform the respondent of the right to attend, present evidence, be represented by counsel, and the deadline (e.g., notify within fifteen days) for contesting the proposed action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the notice identifies the precise rule/section alleged violated and the proposed term of suspension (if required); failure to timely notify the agency may result in suspension without hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for hearing and application for more definite statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A respondent may request a hearing and apply for a more definite statement specifying particularities of the notice (e.g., citation and particular section of the fire code alleged violated, time of alleged violation, and term of proposed suspension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File promptly and identify the specific clarifications sought so the agency can amend the notice appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of notice / more definite statement (what to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: When amending a notice in response to a request for more definite statement, the agency should add specifics such as the proposed term of suspension and precise revision of subsection language to identify the exact code sections, time, and factual details of the alleged violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide precise statutory or code citations and factual particulars (dates, times, specific code provisions violated, and descriptive facts) in the amended notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion for summary decision grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may move for summary decision (dismissal) on the ground that no evidence exists to establish an essential fact required for the agency action (e.g., no evidence that the premises could contain at least 50 persons to constitute a Class C place of assembly under the Life Safety Code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the essential factual threshold and demonstrate the absence of evidence; cite legal standard for summary decision and applicable code definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and terms of consent orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A consent order may include an agency reprimand, agreed remedial measures by respondent (e.g., installation of signage), and dismissal of further proceedings concerning the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft clear agreed terms, specify remedial actions with measurable requirements (e.g., letter size for a sign), and include signature blocks for agency and respondent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition for declaratory ruling contents and occupancy standards
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for declaratory ruling should present: petitioner's name/address, facts presented (detailed description of premises and use), rules involved, the question presented, petitioner's contention (legal argument), and the ruling requested. Substantive example: Life Safety Code defines a Class C place of assembly as capacity 50–300 persons; capacity is determined by maximum occupancy load calculated in section 8-1.5.1 as 7 square feet per person for concentrated use (dance floor) and 15 square feet per person for less concentrated use (drinking establishment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When seeking a declaratory ruling on occupancy, argue whether the usual/customary use or an occasional more concentrated use controls occupancy calculation; provide precise measurements, seating counts, examples of occasional use, and legal rationale for the preferred method of calculation.
